method: Desk research across four parallel streams: (1) green ammonia production capex/opex, (2) production cost for the other five fuels, (3) port storage and bunkering, (4) vessel dual-fuel premiums, merchant prices and FX. Priority followed the sensitivity ranking in the brief: e-ammonia production capex and opex first, then merchant price, then port storage, bunkering and the vessel premium. Production capex is expressed as USD per tonne-per-annum at a stated reference nameplate, never as a flat scalar. Every production block was normalised to one common scope - a complete export-ready complex including dedicated renewables - because the single largest error found was scope mismatch, not level; where the underlying source covered a narrower boundary the adder and its arithmetic are recorded in the relevant source note. Capex figures are real 2025 USD; merchant prices are nominal at their stated assessment date (Aug 2026 for LSFO, LNG and biofuel, Mar-Jul 2026 for ammonia and methanol) and are deliberately NOT deflated to 2025. Deliberately excluded: the vessel catalogue, fuelEmissions, imoNetZero defaults and the country WACC rows. Nothing here was tuned to reproduce the MMMCZCS Chilean copper corridor study; where our figures disagree with it that disagreement is reported. Note on orientation: every {low, central, high} in this file is strictly ascending EXCEPT scaleExponent, which preserves the existing bundle's descending convention (existing band low 0.70 / central 0.65 / high 0.60), so scaleExponent.low holds the numerically larger exponent (less discount at scale) and scaleExponent.high the smaller (more discount). This orientation has not been inverted.
openQuestions: The $1,400/tpa figure attributed to NEOM in packages/corridor-schema/src/ref/bundle.ts is not derivable from any published NEOM number in any unit. NEOM at financial close is $8.4bn for 1.2 Mt/yr = $7,000/tpa NH3, or $3,818/kW of electrolyser, or $38,400 per t-H2/yr. The '1,400' almost certainly originates from IRENA's renewable ammonia PRODUCTION cost range of 'USD 720 - 1 400 per tonne' (Innovation Outlook: Renewable Ammonia, 2022, p.16) or from IRENA's PEM electrolyser system cost of '700-1 400' USD/kW (Green Hydrogen Cost Reduction, 2020, Table ES1) - a flow read as a stock, or a $/kW read as a $/tpa. It should be deleted, not re-scoped: IRENA's capital intensity for a conventional NATURAL GAS ammonia plant is USD 1,500-2,000 per annual tonne, so $1,400/tpa is below the floor for a grey plant and cannot describe a green one under any scope definition.

The $1,100m / 60,000 t-yr line item attributed to MMMCZCS could not be found in the public document. We read 'Chilean Green Corridors - Copper Concentrate Export' (MMMCZCS, 11 Sep 2025) in full: it gives 60,000 t/yr of ammonia, a $2.85bn green-corridor 15-year lifetime NPV, an $850m fossil counterfactual, ~$80/t on the product and a ~$2,000m gap - but no $1,100m line item, no plant/vessel/bunkering split, no currency year, no electrolyser MW and no LCOA. $18,333/tpa is therefore UNVERIFIED AT SOURCE, notwithstanding that our independent bottom-up on the study's own described configuration (200 ha Atacama PV, electrolysis, ASU, Haber-Bosch, refrigerated tanks) lands at $14,500-20,000/tpa and reproduces it without being tuned to it.

A second, non-excludable reading of that $1,100m: since the $2.85bn is explicitly a 15-year lifetime NPV, an internal component may be too. $1,100m / (60,000 t/yr x 15 yr) = $1,222 per tonne PRODUCED, which sits inside IRENA's $720-1,400/t and Deloitte/GIZ's $916-1,350/t. Under that reading the bundle's $1,400 and the study's implied $18,333 are the same quantity, differing only by whether you divide by lifetime output or by one year's nameplate. We favour the capex reading (see the findings note) but cannot exclude this one from the public document.

prodNameplateTonnesPerYear is declared in the schema and populated in the data but no code reads it, so production cost resolves as a flat scalar and a 15 kt/yr corridor is charged the same as a 600 kt/yr one. Fixing the level without fixing the scaling relocates the error rather than removing it. Recommendation in the findings note: reuse the existing build-here machinery (scale exponents, FOAK multiplier, firming) for the build-plant path rather than writing a second mechanism.

The model's fossil/green split is the wrong axis for port infrastructure. LNG is fossil and needs a full cryogenic terminal plus a $55-90m bunker vessel; the correct split is incumbent-infrastructure (LSFO ~ $0) versus new-infrastructure (everything else). Setting portStorageCapexUsdM to $0 for 'fossil' is only right for LSFO.

vesselCapexPremium cannot be a single fraction across segments. The ammonia dual-fuel fuel system is a roughly fixed dollar cost of order $20-25m for a deep-sea vessel, so the premium as a FRACTION scales inversely with hull value: 16% on a $150m 15,000 TEU boxship (DNV 2025 and MMMCZCS 2022 agree exactly), ~26% on a $73.5m Newcastlemax, ~30%+ on a $37m Kamsarmax. The bundle's 0.25 is close to right for bulk carriers and roughly 1.6x too high for large container ships. Consider carrying a fixed USD adder instead of a fraction.

No published ammonia bunker price assessment exists at any port as of Aug 2026, despite commercial ammonia bunkering having begun. Any ammonia bunker price in the model is necessarily commodity price plus an assumed bunkering margin, and that margin is not sourced here.

No LH2 bunkering cost of any kind exists - vessel, terminal or shore equipment - because nothing has been built. Every lh2 bunkering number in this file is an analogy from cryogenic cost multipliers and is marked unverified. The lh2 vesselCapexPremium is worse: there is no merchant LH2 orderbook at all (DNV AFI recorded one hydrogen order in all of 1H-2026), so the value carried is the ammonia dual-fuel bulker premium used as an explicit FLOOR, repeated in all three positions. It is not an LH2 estimate and must not be read as one.

Bunker vessel OPERATING costs could not be sourced for any fuel. Moore OpCost and Drewry Ship Operating Costs were not retrievable. All bunkering opexUsdMPerYear values here are estimates built from a $6,000-10,000/day crewed-coastal-vessel assumption. Note also that expressing barge opex as a fixed percentage of capex is structurally wrong for this asset class - crew, class, insurance and P&I scale with vessel size and manning, not with the cost of the containment system, so a percentage rule makes cryogenic fuels look worse than they are.

IRENA 2022 Table 11 ('Capital cost for renewable ammonia plants, including or excluding renewable energy generation cost', Annex C, p.134) is the single most directly relevant published table for the headline number and it was NOT read - every retrieval truncated before the table body and direct PDF download was blocked. The same applies to Table 10 (p.133) and to Deloitte/GIZ H2Uppp 2024 Tables 24, 27 and 28 (pp.56-59), which cover a 600 kt/yr complex at exactly the scope required here. If those tables can be obtained, capexUsdPerTpa for e-ammonia should be revisited before this bundle is published.

The 2017 USD to 2025 USD escalator (x1.40) and the 2020 EUR to 2025 EUR escalator (x1.25) used in the port storage derivations are CEPCI-type assumptions that were not verified against a retrieved index. They move the ammonia and LH2 terminal numbers materially.

The methanol terminal figure carries an unresolved 2.2x disagreement. TNO 2023 R11326 Table D.1 reads '3 assets, installed capacity 31,6 kton' for the import archetype and '4 assets, 114 kton, 50.000m3' for the export archetype, which is internally inconsistent (4 x 50,000 m3 is about 158 kt, not 114 kt). Whether 31.6 kt is total or per tank swings the derived unit cost from EUR 1,027/m3 to EUR 342/m3. No European methanol marine terminal has published a capex figure - Mabanaft Hamburg and Evos Rotterdam both declined to disclose.

Currency-year normalisation is incomplete by design. Production capex is stated as real 2025 USD but several underlying project figures are as-spent nominal across 2020-2026 (NEOM 2023, AM Green 2026, Kasso 2022, Neste Rotterdam 2024) and were not deflated to a common basis, because process-plant escalation (CEPCI / IHS UCCI) diverged sharply from CPI over 2020-2025 and applying a CPI deflator would have introduced a larger error than it removed.

LNG is carried with a non-zero production capex because a liquefaction plant is a real build, unlike LSFO. If the corridor model prices LNG at a MERCHANT bunker price it must not also charge liquefaction capex - the capital is already in the price and charging both double-counts. The same trap applies to LSFO and is the reason its production block is zero. Ensure the build-plant and buy-fuel paths remain mutually exclusive per fuel.

A cross-check that reads oddly and is left unresolved rather than smoothed: on the per-tonne basis the brief asks about, lh2 is 4.9x more capital-intensive than e-ammonia as it should be, but on a DELIVERED-ENERGY basis the ordering inverts - lh2 is about $450 per (GJ/yr) against e-ammonia's about $591. Two causes, both real and neither an arithmetic error. First, scope asymmetry: the e-ammonia block includes refrigerated ammonia storage and a jetty, the lh2 block explicitly excludes a jetty, and ammonia additionally buys an ASU and a Haber-Bosch synloop that hydrogen does not. Second, reference size: the e-ammonia 100,000 t/yr reference is small and FOAK-loaded, and the two reference nameplates are close on energy (1.86 PJ/yr for ammonia against 2.19 PJ/yr for hydrogen) so the scale penalty does not cancel. Expressed per tonne of embodied hydrogen the numbers are e-ammonia about $61,950 and lh2 about $54,000 per t-H2/yr, which is the ordering the physics implies. Do not read the per-GJ figure as evidence that liquid hydrogen is the cheaper corridor - the port storage row, where lh2 costs 8.4x ammonia, and the absence of any buildable LH2 bunker chain both point the other way.

The e-methanol production capex anchor is weaker than its position in the table suggests. Neither European Energy nor Mitsui has ever published a construction cost for Kasso, the only completed commercial-scale e-methanol plant in the West; the DKK 1.5bn figure in general circulation traces to one Danish trade outlet in Nov 2022, before construction. That is why the block is marked unverified despite the plant being real and operating. Every other e-methanol datapoint is either an abandoned project (FlagshipONE, a floor not a cost), a bankruptcy (Liquid Wind), or Chinese capacity with no published cost.

Production scope was normalised to include dedicated renewables for e-ammonia, e-methanol and lh2 so the three are comparable. For e-methanol and lh2 this required an adder to the sourced conversion-island figure; the arithmetic is in each block's source notes. The island-only figures (e-methanol $2,500/$5,000/$8,000 per tpa; lh2 $18,000/$35,000/$60,000 per tpa H2) are what the sources actually print, and should be used instead if the model supplies power from the grid rather than building generation.

sources.note: Zero is a modelling convention, not a measurement, which is why this block is marked unverified. LSFO is the residual co-product of a refinery configured around transport fuels; no refinery is built because of marine demand. IMO 2020, the largest specification change the bunker market has ever seen, was met without a single refinery being built for it. The IEA data is cited to establish the surplus-capacity condition that makes the marginal-cost framing correct, not to supply a cost. No citable document was found that makes the attribute-zero-capex-to-bunkers argument directly; it is constructed here from IEA capacity/demand data plus standard refinery economics.

sources.title: Ammonia to Power: Forecasting the Levelized Cost of Electricity from Green Ammonia in Large-scale Power Plants
sources.publisher: University of Oxford, Department of Engineering Science (Cesaro, Ives, Nayak-Luke, Mason, Banares-Alcantara)
sources.figureUsed: 'Haber-Bosch CAPEX 3,300 USD per kg NH3/hr'; 'ASU 1,450 USD per kg N2/hr' (2020 USD)
sources.note: Our conversion, and it is the decisive one for the scope argument: 1 kg NH3/hr x 8,760 h = 8.76 t/yr, so Haber-Bosch is $3,300/8.76 = $377/tpa at 100% capacity factor, $419/tpa at 90%. N2 mass fraction of NH3 = 14.0067/17.0305 = 0.8224, so ASU is $1,450 x 0.8224 / 8.76 = $136/tpa at 100%, $151/tpa at 90%. ASU plus synloop together is about $570/tpa at scale. The classic process-plant portion of a green ammonia complex is therefore only about 8% of NEOM's $7,000/tpa - everything else is renewables, electrolysis, storage, export and EPC. This is why the scope question is decided by what generation is inside the boundary, not by whether the synloop is.

sources.title: Innovation Outlook: Renewable Ammonia
sources.locator: p.16, Summary for Policy Makers; capital-intensity statements in the same report
sources.figureUsed: 'Renewable ammonia production costs for new plants are estimated to be in the range of USD 720 - 1 400 per tonne today, falling to USD 310-610 per tonne by 2050'; 'The capital intensity of a natural gas-based ammonia plant is typically USD 1 500 to USD 2 000 per tonne' (per annual tonne); 'The capital intensity of a coal-based ammonia plant is around USD 2 900 per annual tonne'
sources.note: Cited for two purposes. First, the $720-1,400/t range is a LEVELISED PRODUCTION COST per tonne produced, 2020 USD - it is the most likely origin of the bundle's $1,400 and it must not be used as a capex per annual tonne. Second, the natural-gas capital intensity of $1,500-2,000 per ANNUAL tonne is the sanity floor: a green plant buys everything a grey plant buys except the reformer, plus electrolysers, plus hundreds of MW to GW of dedicated generation, so $1,400/tpa is below the floor for a grey plant and cannot be a green complete-complex capex under any scope. Cross-check on our own recommendation: at 8% real WACC, 25-year life (CRF 0.0937) and 90% utilisation, $11,000/tpa with 5.5% opex gives an LCOA of $1,817/t at 100 kt - honestly expensive because of small scale - while the same formula on NEOM's $7,000/tpa gives $1,156/t, which lands inside this source's $720-1,400/t range. The framework reproduces the published large-scale LCOA range, which is the check that matters. NOT READ: Table 10 (p.133) and Table 11 (p.134, 'Capital cost for renewable ammonia plants, including or excluding renewable energy generation cost') - every retrieval truncated before the table bodies and direct PDF download was blocked. sources.title: Global Hydrogen Review 2025
sources.figureUsed: 'USD 2 000 to USD 2 600 per kilowatt (kW)' installed electrolyser cost outside China, 2024 USD; 'USD 1 500 to USD 2 400 per kW' for Chinese units installed outside China
sources.note: Reference nameplate is 18,250 t/yr of H2 (50 t/day), so capexUsdPerTpa is PER TONNE OF HYDROGEN, not per tonne of a carrier. The island-only build-up from the underlying research (electrolysis plus liquefaction plus cryogenic storage, EXCLUDING generation) is 18,000 / 35,000 / 60,000 USD per tpa H2. WE HAVE NORMALISED UPWARD to include dedicated renewables so this row is scope-comparable with e-ammonia and e-methanol. Our arithmetic: 18,250 t H2/yr at 53 kWh/kg is 967 GWh/yr for electrolysis plus about 183 GWh/yr for liquefaction at 10 kWh/kg, about 1,150 GWh/yr total; at a 40% hybrid renewable capacity factor that is about 328 MW; at about $1,050/kW installed that is about $344m, or about $18,850 per tpa of H2. Adding that to the island-only band gives 30,000 / 54,000 / 90,000. Low case is high-capacity-factor grid power with Chinese stacks at $1,500/kW landed and 2021-era liquefier pricing; high case is a low capacity factor (about 0.35) with Western stacks at $2,600/kW and a liquefier at the top of the DOE literature range. Opex is 3.5-4% of capex: IEA gives 3% fixed opex for water electrolysis and we apply 4% to the liquefaction block for rotating machinery, cold-box integrity and LN2 pre-cooling. This EXCLUDES electricity, which at 53 plus 10 = 63 kWh/kg is by far the dominant cost of LH2 and belongs in the energy model. SANITY CHECK: lh2 is more capital-intensive per tonne than e-ammonia by 4.9x on these central figures, as it must be - though note that on a delivered-energy basis (120 GJ/t for H2 against 18.6 for NH3) the gap narrows to about 1.1x per GJ, and it is the energy basis that means something for a corridor.

sources.title: Current Status of Hydrogen Liquefaction Costs, DOE Hydrogen Program Record 19001
sources.publisher: US Department of Energy (record describes the HDSAM liquefier cost basis; model at https://hdsam.es.anl.gov/index.php?content=hdsam)
sources.locator: liquefier capital cost curve fit, C in tonnes/day
sources.figureUsed: liquefier capital cost relation of the form 5.6 x C^0.8, i.e. an explicit scale exponent of 0.8 for hydrogen liquefaction
sources.note: Basis for the scale exponent. The exponent is ultimately HDSAM's, but the HDSAM landing page is a model-download page publishing no cost equation, so Record 19001 is the citable document. Electrolysis is modular and does not deflate with scale beyond procurement leverage (n about 0.95); liquefaction has this published 0.8. At about a 65:35 capex weighting the blend is about 0.90 - HIGHER (less favourable) than a classic process plant precisely because the electrolyser dominates. DO NOT APPLY 0.6-0.7 TO LH2. THE BLOCK IS MARKED UNVERIFIED for a specific and important reason: the IEA's Global Hydrogen Review 2024 Assumptions Annex prints 'CAPEX USD/t H2/day NA' and 'OPEX USD/t H2/day NA' for liquefaction - withheld for confidentiality - so the single most-cited source in the field publishes no liquefaction capex at all, and the cryogenic storage component here ($3,000/tpa within the build-up) is an estimate rather than a sourced figure. Buildability is also a constraint the model should respect: the largest operating liquefiers globally are about 30-35 t/day, no one has built an electrolytic LH2 plant above about 50 t/day, and the flagship LH2 export project (HESC) has had its Australian scope put under review.

sources.title: The Future of Hydrogen - Assumptions Annex
sources.locator: transmission, distribution and storage assumptions table (exact table number not confirmed)
sources.figureUsed: LH2 import terminal: capacity per tank '3,550 tH2', CAPEX per tank 'USD 320 million', electricity 0.2 kWh/kgH2, boil-off '0.1%/day'; LH2 export terminal: '3,190 tH2', 'USD 290 million', annual OPEX '4% of CAPEX'
sources.note: Our derivation: $320m / 3,550 t = $90,141 per tonne of H2 stored = $6,382/m3 at 70.8 kg/m3 (2017 USD). Scaled to the 1,550 t working volume implied by 15,500 t/yr throughput at 10 turnovers, using exponent 0.65, gives $187m in 2017 USD; escalated at x1.40 gives about $261m, rounded to a central of 270. Cross-fuel check from the same table: LH2 costs $751 per GJ stored against ammonia's $92 - 8.2x per unit of energy and 5.5x per m3. GREATER-THAN-2x DISAGREEMENT REPORTED, NOT AVERAGED: $6,382/m3 (IEA, 50,000 m3 scale) against about EUR 41,000/m3 (TNO 2023, at a 1,440 m3 scale) against $8,000/m3 (Thunder Said, 'small-scale') is a 6x spread driven almost entirely by scale, and none of the sources publishes a scaling law. UNVERIFIED also because of buildability: 15,500 t/yr at this energy basis needs about 21,890 m3 of tankage, against a stated industry maximum of 'about 20,000 m3' (Hydrogen Import Coalition, 2021, p.18), Kawasaki's Kobe terminal at 2,500 m3 and NASA's largest-in-the-world sphere at about 4,700 m3 - so this is roughly five tanks of the largest size ever constructed. The model should carry either a very high capex or a hard availability constraint for LH2. Boil-off at 0.1%/day is 3.7%/yr of throughput, which is a product loss the model should account separately.

Our derivation: LH2 containment costs roughly 3-5x LNG per m3 (consistent with this source's cryogenic multiplier and with the IEA's 5.5x LH2:NH3 per-m3 ratio), giving $15,000-25,000/m3, so $45-75m for 3,000 m3 and $75-125m for 5,000 m3. sources.title: Global Hydrogen Review 2026 - Production
sources.figureUsed: 2030 costs: northern China green hydrogen 'below USD 2/kg'; Europe about 'USD 3.5/kg'; Middle East, India and Chile 'just above USD 3/kg'; blue with CCUS 'potentially just above USD 1/kg', described as largely theoretical
sources.note: DERIVED, NOT ASSESSED - there is no liquid-hydrogen marine bunker market and no published LH2 bunker price assessment anywhere, which is why this block is unverified. Our build-up: gaseous green H2 at the plant gate today USD 3.5-6.0/kg (today's costs sit above the 2030 figures printed above); liquefaction adds an energy penalty of about 30% of the H2 LHV plus capex, conventionally +USD 1.0-2.0/kg; storage, boil-off (0.2-1%/day at 20 K), transport and bunkering margin add +USD 0.5-1.5/kg. That gives USD 5,000-9,500/t with a central of 7,500. On an LHV basis (120 GJ/t) that is USD 42-79/GJ, against VLSFO at USD 16-20/GJ and delivered LNG at USD 23-28/GJ. State clearly in any model output that this figure has NO market observation behind it. Corroborating the absence of a market: DNV Alternative Fuels Insight recorded exactly one hydrogen-fuelled vessel order in all of 1H-2026 against 73 for LNG, and Lloyd's Register noted in Jan 2026 that hydrogen bunkering facilities remain limited.

sources.title: Alternative-fuel vessel orders fall in 1H 2026: DNV
sources.publisher: Argus Media, reporting DNV Alternative Fuels Insight

Rather than invent a spread, the single figure carried here is the AMMONIA dual-fuel bulk carrier premium of 0.26, repeated in all three positions and used as an explicit FLOOR: LH2 tankage is roughly 4x the volume of HFO and cryogenic at 20 K, so the true value is certainly higher, and it is unknown. If the model can represent 'not established', prefer that to this floor.

sources.title: Euro foreign exchange reference rates - US dollar (USD), series EXR.D.USD.EUR.SP00.A
sources.figureUsed: 1.1567 USD per EUR (14 Aug 2026); recent dailies 13 Aug 1.1534, 12 Aug 1.1545, 11 Aug 1.1540, 10 Aug 1.1555
sources.note: The bundle's 1.08 is 6.6% too low: converting a EUR-denominated regulatory cost at 1.08 instead of 1.1567 understates the USD cost by (1.1567-1.08)/1.1567 = 6.63%. WHICH RATE IS CORRECT: neither same-day spot nor a rolling average. EU ETS allowances are bought through the year, so the effective rate is a volume-weighted average across the purchase window; FuelEU Maritime penalties are defined in euros and assessed annually against a full calendar year of voyages, so converting a year's accrued liability at one day's spot mismatches the accrual period. Use the ECB ANNUAL AVERAGE for historical compliance years and a flat forward rate at the current level (1.15-1.16) for projection years, and expose it as a sensitivity - a 5-10% FX move is the same order of magnitude as many of the technology assumptions in this file and should not be a hard-coded constant. ADJACENT AND PROBABLY NEEDED: the EU ETS allowance price was 72 EUR/tCO2 in Apr 2026 and averaged 74.04 EUR/tCO2 in May 2026 (December 2026 contract), with a 12-month forward projection of about 78.65; at 1.1567 that is about USD 86.75/tCO2 for 75 EUR. A dated August 2026 EUA spot settlement could NOT be retrieved - ICE and EEX daily settlements are paywalled - so refresh from EEX before publishing. Note also that maritime EU ETS reached a 100% surrender obligation for 2026 emissions, so no 40%/70% phase-in factor should apply from 2026 onward.
